meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Even if I knew that tomorrow the world would go to pieces, I would still plant my apple tree'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to MLK Jr. and to Martin Luther, but documented in neither. The earliest trace is a 1944 Confessing Church circular; the true author is unknown.

answer.label: Not Martin Luther King Jr. — and almost certainly not Martin Luther either
answer.sourceLine: This line is popularly pinned on Martin Luther King Jr., and even more often on the 16th-century reformer Martin Luther — but it is found in the works of neither. Its earliest documented appearance is a German Confessing Church circular of October 1944, and the Luther scholar Martin Schloemann, who wrote a whole book about it, concluded it cannot be traced to Luther. The German original is “Wenn ich wüsste, dass morgen die Welt unterginge, würde ich heute noch ein Apfelbäumchen pflanzen.”

source.heading: A wartime saying, not a King (or Luther) quotation

source.excerpt:
“Even if I knew that tomorrow the world would go to pieces, I would still plant my apple tree.”

German original: “Wenn ich wüsste, dass morgen die Welt unterginge, würde ich heute noch ein Apfelbäumchen pflanzen.”
trail: The saying is first documented in October 1944, in a circular letter of the Confessing Church in Hesse by Pastor Karl Lotz — nearly four centuries after Luther’s death and years before it was ever tied to Martin Luther King Jr.

The Luther scholar Martin Schloemann examined the phrase at book length in Luthers Apfelbäumchen? and found it nowhere in Luther’s writings, arguing it grew from a 19th-century sentimental image of Luther the garden-tending householder.
Dedicated quote-research (Zitatforschung) reaches the same verdict: an apocryphal Luther saying with no source before the Second World War.
Fact-checkers list it among statements faked or misquoted under Martin Luther King Jr.’s name, a confusion helped along by the shared name.
source.excerptNote: The English version circulating under Martin Luther King Jr.’s name is a modern, anonymous translation of the German saying — not a passage from any King sermon, letter, or book.

author.name: Martin Luther
author.kicker: The figure the saying is pinned on
author.heading: Martin Luther — who never wrote it
author.bio: Martin Luther was the German monk and theologian whose 1517 protest sparked the Protestant Reformation and whose Bible translation shaped modern German. The apple-tree saying attached itself to him only in the 20th century, drawing on a sentimental image of Luther as a serene garden-keeping householder; scholars note that the real Luther anticipated the world’s end with more eagerness than the quote’s calm suggests. It is not found anywhere in his voluminous writings.

misattribution.heading: Two Martins, one saying, neither the source
misattribution.intro: The line is a favorite of inspirational posts, where it is stamped with the name of either Martin Luther King Jr. or Martin Luther — a slippage the shared name makes easy. Neither attribution holds up.

items.why: The sentence appears in none of King’s sermons, books, or letters, yet quote sites such as Goodreads post it under his name, and fact-checkers list it among statements faked or misquoted under his name.
Though far more often credited to him, the saying is absent from Luther’s works and first surfaces only in 1944; Martin Schloemann’s study concludes it was retrofitted onto Luther after the fact.

misattribution.truthLine: The oldest known version is German, from a Confessing Church circular of October 1944 — a message of hope amid wartime ruin whose actual author remains unknown.

context.heading: Why it caught on
lead: The saying spread because it distills a very modern consolation — keep doing the ordinary, life-affirming work even under the shadow of catastrophe. That resonance is exactly why it was reached for in the rubble of 1944 Germany, and why it keeps getting re-credited to famous moral authorities like the two Martins.

A kindred, much older sentiment survives in Jewish tradition — Rabbi Yohanan ben Zakkai’s counsel that if you hold a sapling and hear the Messiah has come, you should plant the sapling first — but that parallel is a thematic echo, not the documented source of the German wording.
context.pull: A hopeful thought that outgrew whoever first said it.
